_note: Narration script for the Headache module (CPP-061-AO v1.0, CPP-047-AO). Lee voice on eleven_v4, one take, short conversational sentences. The prompt sent to ElevenLabs starts with the [calmly] tag and spells EOC as "E O C", ROSIER as "Rosier", ODT as "O D T", and HIV as "H I V"; captions use the text here.

lines.head: Introduction
sentences: Headache.
What every Ambulance Officer needs to know.

lines.head: Two kinds
sentences: Most headaches are primary. Migraine, tension or cluster headaches.
But about 1 in 20 is secondary.
A bleed, an infection, a head injury, or rising pressure in the skull.
Your job isn't to diagnose it. It's to spot the warning signs.

lines.head: Assess
sentences: Start with basic care.
Take a good history. It's your best tool.
Then a pain and neuro assessment, including ROSIER and their walk.
Similar headaches before, with the same triggers? That's reassuring.

lines.head: Red flags
sentences: Now look for red flags.
A sudden thunderclap headache. Or one brought on by coughing, exertion or sex.
Fever, a stiff neck, a rash, vomiting or confusion.
Any neuro sign, even if it's gone.
A first severe headache over 50.
A new headache with cancer or HIV.
One that's getting worse over hours or days.
Severe headache in pregnancy.
A recent head knock.
Or worse lying down, or on waking, with vomiting.

lines.head: Any red flag
sentences: Find one? Prioritise transport and request clinical support.
No support available? Consult the EOC Clinician.
Neuro signs on ROSIER? Follow the stroke protocol.
Suspected infection? Follow the sepsis protocol.

lines.head: Treat the symptoms
sentences: Encourage their own migraine plan and medicines.
Give pain relief as per the pain protocol.
Nauseated? Consider ondansetron, 4 milligrams, dissolved on the tongue.
And remember. Feeling better doesn't mean it's benign.

lines.head: Transport
sentences: Transport to an appropriate facility.
Thinking of leaving them at home? Consult the EOC Clinician first.
